source.title: The curse of overparametrization in adversarial training: Precise analysis of robust generalization for random features regression

record.file_problem: The main paper and supplementary material are present. The supplement heading names a different paper, but the supplied text is otherwise readable and not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: It studies test risk as random-feature model size varies and reports a non-adversarial double-descent result, but uses a high-dimensional random-features analysis rather than reproducing the original method.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior double-descent results in its introduction and related work; those cited results are not rows. The paper's own results include a non-adversarial standard-risk curve and separate adversarial-risk curves. The latter measure robust risk under perturbed inputs, not ordinary test error, so they are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study derives its own asymptotic risk formula for random-features regression and checks it against gradient-descent runs (d=100, n=300). In the non-adversarial limit (ε→0) the standard test-error curve shows double descent, peaking at N/n=1 and minimised at infinite overparametrization. That bears on the general double-descent curve. The paper's main subject is adversarial risk, which is a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors derive exact asymptotic adversarial risk for adversarially trained random-features regression. Without an adversary they recover standard double descent, with the peak at N/n=1 and the best error at infinite size. With an adversary, higher overparametrization generally hurts robust generalization, the risk peak shifts right as ε grows, and adversarial training can act as a beneficial regularizer for standard risk.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random-features regression with a randomly fixed first layer and learned second-layer weights; the main analysis is robust ERM in a proportional high-dimensional limit. The non-adversarial ERM case is included as a special case.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported risk curves depend on adversarial perturbation/training strength ε, noise variance τ², and the sample-to-dimension ratio ψ2. The paper also reports different peak locations as ε changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial risk versus N/n can have a finite optimum, rise-then-fall shapes that stay above the zero-estimator risk, or rise monotonically, depending on ε, τ² and ψ2. Its peak shifts right as ε grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In adversarially trained random-features regression, overparametrization generally hurts robust risk, and the robust-risk curve departs from standard double descent in an adversary-strength-dependent way.

fits_no_version.finding: With no test-time adversary (εtest=0), adversarial training with ε>0 lowers standard risk, acting as a regularizer. The optimal ε grows with overparametrization (Fig. 5b,d).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training acts as a regularizer that reduces standard risk, more strongly at higher overparametrization.

record.problems: The empirical comparison described for Figure 2 is limited to d=100 and n=300, and the text and caption disagree on whether dots average 20 or 100 trials. Many other displayed curves are theoretical predictions rather than reported empirical runs. The explicit standard-risk formula is restricted to the underparameterized regime.
record.rows_left_out: No reported model-size, sample-size, or test-risk result bearing on the claim was left out. Values available only in plots are retained as figure-only or summarized where the text explicitly describes the trend.

untested.parts: Not tested. No trained deep networks; only random-features regression.
Not tested. No epoch or training-time sweeps.
Sample-size dependence is characterised only for n>N. Whether more data hurts as n approaches N from below is not tested.
Only one model class (random features, shifted ReLU, Gaussian linear teacher). Other classes are not tested.
Not tested. No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.

Not tested on the standard-risk curve. Fig. 3 shows ε≈0 curves at τ²=0, 0.5 and 5, but the text does not analyse noise dependence of the standard-risk peak, multiple peaks, or removal of the peak by optimal regularization.

missing.what: In the non-adversarial case (ε=0), the standard-risk peak occurs at the interpolation threshold N/n=1, shown for τ²=0, 0.5 and 5 with ψ2=3.
With ε≈0 the standard generalization error is minimised at infinite overparametrization, across ψ2 values.

record.verdict_notes: Most curves are theoretical predictions; the empirical check is limited to d=100, n=300. The ε→0 double-descent result reproduces the Mei–Montanari prediction for random features rather than original deep-network evidence, so V1 is left untested. The record's V3 'challenges' label was removed because the n>N regime cannot show the effect V3 describes.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model size only for shifted-ReLU random features regression; it does not test epoch-wise descent or a broad range of deep-network architectures.
Training-epoch or training-time sweeps are not reported.
The sample-size result is for non-adversarial standard risk in the underparameterized regime; it does not test whether more data can hurt robust risk near interpolation.
The study tests random features regression, not whether the curve generalizes across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and samples.

The paper varies noise and adversary settings in robust-risk analyses, but does not test whether label noise drives the ordinary test-error peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to assess whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
